Bug_Title: Regex patterns following a possessive quantifier should not always fail
Bug_Details:
Possessive quantifiers in Regex patterns like below improve performance by eliminating needless backtracking:
?+ , *+ , ++ , {n}+ , {n,}+ , {n,m}+
But because possessive quantifiers do not keep backtracking positions and never give back, the following sub-patterns should not match only similar
characters. Otherwise, possessive quantifiers consume all characters that could have matched the following sub-patterns and nothing remains for the
following sub-patterns.
Noncompliant code example
Pattern pattern1 = Pattern.compile("a++abc");       // Noncompliant, the second 'a' never matches
Pattern pattern2 = Pattern.compile("\\d*+[02468]"); // Noncompliant, the sub-pattern "[02468]" never matches
Compliant solution
Pattern pattern1 = Pattern.compile("aa++bc");            // Compliant, for example it can match "aaaabc"
Pattern pattern2 = Pattern.compile("\\d*+(?<=[02468])"); // Compliant, for example it can match an even number like "1234"
Bug_Explanation: The regex patterns use possessive quantifiers which consume all characters greedily without leaving any for subsequent sub-patterns, resulting in no matches. In 'a++abc', the 'a++' consumes all 'a's, leaving none for the 'abc' to match. Similarly, in '\d*+[02468]', '\d*+' consumes all digits, leaving none to match the trailing '[02468]'.
Trigger_Explanation: The JUnit test cases fail because the possessive quantifiers in the regex patterns consume all characters greedily without allowing the following sub-patterns to match. Thus, in testShowBug1, 'a++' consumes all 'a's, leaving none for 'abc' to match. Similarly, in testShowBug2, '\d*+' consumes all digits, leaving none for '[02468]' to match, causing both tests to fail.
